screens.title: SD-WAN Monitoring, Troubleshooting, and Operations
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how to observe, diagnose, and maintain a Cisco SD-WAN deployment using vManage and device-level tools. We start with the dashboards and reports that give you a live and historical view of device health, TLOC and link quality, and application performance. Then we'll practice common troubleshooting flows: reading alarms, running remote diagnostics from vManage, and using essential CLI show commands on vEdge and cEdge devices. You will also see how to stage software images and perform upgrades safely, and how to collect a support bundle when escalation is required. These operational skills matter because SD-WAN is a dynamic fabric: paths and policies change, certificates and time synchronization affect control-plane trust, and proactive monitoring prevents outages. As an example, you will follow a simulated "device down" scenario where an expired certificate plus NTP drift breaks control connections; learning to trace from the vManage alarm to CLI checks shortens mean time to repair. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the right dashboard or CLI command for the problem, perform safe upgrades, and collect diagnostic artifacts for deeper analysis. Remember: good monitoring replaces guesswork with data.

screens.title: vManage Dashboards Explained
screens.narratorSegment: vManage dashboards are your single pane of glass into the SD-WAN fabric. A dashboard groups widgets that surface device health, control-plane connectivity, TLOC and WAN link statistics, application SLA compliance, and alarms. Think of dashboards as both a daily operations cockpit and an incident triage map: they help you spot failing devices, saturated interfaces, and applications missing their SLAs. For example, when you see a spike in jitter on a TLOC color used for voice, that single widget points you to the affected sites and the time window for deeper investigation. Dashboards are customizable. You will build or adjust them to surface the metrics you care about, such as C P U thresholds or particular application classes. A common misconception is that dashboards alone resolve incidents; they do not. Dashboards show where to look, not how to fix it. Use dashboards first to narrow scope, then gather logs and run real-time diagnostics. In practice, pair a dashboard alarm with a time-correlated support bundle or CLI output before making configuration changes. How might you tune a dashboard to reduce false positives while still catching real degradation?

screens.title: Key Metrics to Monitor
screens.narratorSegment: Knowing which metrics to monitor lets you separate noise from signal. At the device level focus on C P U and memory utilization and interface status: sustained high C P U often precedes control-plane problems, and interface errors point to physical or routing issues. For link quality monitor TLOC metrics—latency, jitter, and packet loss—for each TLOC color because AAR uses these values to make path choices. Application performance requires SLA compliance metrics and application-route statistics so you can verify whether an application meets its latency and loss targets. A useful monitoring process is to set thresholds and watch both instantaneous values and trends: a single spike may be transient, while a gradual increase in packet loss signals a degrading link. A common misconception is that high utilization always means failure. Instead, correlate utilization with errors and SLA breaches before reconfiguring. For example, 80 percent interface utilization with low packet loss may be acceptable, but 20 percent packet loss at the same time is not. Regularly export reports for trend analysis and capacity planning. Key Metrics to Monitor means use cpu/memory, interface errors, tloc latency/jitter/loss, and sla compliance as core indicators; always correlate metrics before action.. In practical terms, device health, link quality, and application performance indicators. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Key Metrics
Metrics to watch
Prioritize metrics that affect control-plane trust, data-plane routing, and application SLAs.
Device Health
CPU, memory, and interface errors. Correlate sustained spikes with logs before rebooting devices.
TLOC / Link Quality
Latency, jitter, packet loss per TLOC color. These feed AAR decisions.
Application SLAs
SLA compliance and app-route statistics show real user impact for critical apps.
Process: evaluate before acting
  1. Identify the metric exceeding threshold and record the timestamp.
  2. Correlate with alarms and event logs to find root cause clues.
  3. Run real-time diagnostics (pings, traceroutes, app-route stats) for the affected site and time window.
  4. Decide on mitigation: route change, QoS tweak, or hardware replacement.
Common Mistake

Reacting to a single metric in isolation. Always confirm with logs and SLA data before changing policy or topology.

Key Takeaway

Correlate device, link, and application metrics. Trends show root cause; spikes may be transient.

screens.title: vManage Troubleshooting Tools
screens.narratorSegment: vManage centralizes several troubleshooting capabilities that speed triage. Event logs and alarms aggregate significant occurrences across controllers and edge devices: filter them by severity, device, or time to find root events like certificate failures or control connection losses. Real-time monitoring exposes live graphs of interface utilization, C P U/memory, and TLOC metrics; this helps distinguish transient spikes from sustained problems. A powerful time-saver is remote diagnostics from vManage: you can trigger a ping, traceroute, or even a packet capture on an edge device without SSHing into it. That reduces context switching and preserves a documented trail. However, not all fixes are possible from vManage. In complex cases you must SSH to the edge CLI for commands that show OMP routes, TLOCs, and app-route statistics. A common misconception is thinking remote diagnostics replace CLI checks; instead they complement them. Use vManage to gather evidence quickly, then move to device CLI when you need detailed show output or interactive troubleshooting. Event Logs & Alarms
Filter by severity, device, or time. Look for certificate, NTP, or control connection failures when devices show down.
Real-time Monitoring

Example Workflow

  2. Filter event logs for that device and note the error or reason string.
  3. Run remote ping or packet capture for the time window to confirm link behavior.
  4. If more detail is needed, SSH to the edge device and run show commands.

Start with vManage for quick evidence collection, then transition to CLI for deep diagnostics and fixes.

screens.title: Essential CLI Commands for Edge Devices
screens.narratorSegment: The edge device CLI provides definitive state for control, routing, and application metrics. First, use the command that checks control connections to confirm whether the device has active DTLS or TLS sessions to vSmart and vBond; this reveals whether the control plane is up. Next, OMP routes and TLOC listings show the control-plane learned routes and available transport locators, including TLOC colors and associated metrics—use these to verify route distribution and policy attributes. Application-route statistics give per-application path selection and SLA compliance numbers, which is crucial when Application-Aware Routing behavior is questioned. Other useful commands include seeing policies received from vSmart, interface status, and device logs. A typical sequence when a device is "down" is: check control connections, verify OMP routes and TLOCs, inspect app-route statistics, and review logs. A common misconception is assuming a missing route means policy failed; often the root cause is a missing TLOC or a control-plane disconnect. Practice reading the outputs to map symptoms to causes. Essential CLI Commands for Edge Devices means use control, omp, tloc and app-route commands to confirm control-plane state, route distribution, and application pathing.. Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Essential CLI
Command list and purpose
  • show sdwan control connections — verify control connections to vSmart and vBond, and any certificate reasons for failure.
  • show sdwan omp routes — display OMP learned routes, TLOC attributes, and policy-influenced preferences.
  • show sdwan omp tlocs — list TLOCs with colors and metrics used by AAR.
  • show sdwan app-route statistics — see which path applications use and SLA compliance metrics.
Code Walkthrough: sample commands
show sdwan control connections
show sdwan omp routes
show sdwan omp tlocs
show sdwan app-route statistics
show sdwan policy from-vsmart
show sdwan interface
show logging
request sdwan support-bundle
Practice reading these outputs to map the symptom to the likely cause: control, route distribution, TLOC availability, or application identification.
Pro Tip

Capture the exact timestamps from vManage alarms before running CLI commands so outputs align with the observed event window.

screens.title: vManage Remote Diagnostics vs CLI Access
screens.narratorSegment: Both vManage remote diagnostics and direct CLI access are essential, but they serve different purposes. Use vManage remote tools—remote ping, traceroute, show commands and packet capture—when you need rapid, recorded evidence without changing contexts. These tools are ideal for early triage and for gathering artifacts to attach to incidents. In contrast, SSH access to the vEdge or cEdge CLI is necessary for deep, interactive troubleshooting: inspecting OMP route attributes, checking local policy evaluation, or running fine-grained commands unavailable via vManage. A helpful mental model is to treat vManage as your 'evidence collector' and CLI as your 'repair console.' One misconception is to assume remote diagnostics are always sufficient; sometimes packet captures or show outputs from the device itself reveal details that the remote wrapper does not. For example, an occasional certificate validation failure may only expose full error context in device logs. Practice this decision by starting in vManage for every alarm, and escalate to CLI only when evidence or active remediation is required. vManage Remote Diagnostics vs CLI Access means vmanage for fast evidence and documented traces; cli for deep, interactive troubleshooting and fixes.. In practical terms, when to use vmanage remote tools and when to ssh to the edge device. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common Scenario: Device Not Joining the Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: A device failing to join the fabric is a frequent operational incident. Start by confirming the vManage WAN Edge list or alarm shows the device as down. Next, run the control connections check on the device to see whether DTLS/TLS sessions to vSmart and vBond are up. If the show output indicates "certificate invalid" or similar, verify the certificate status and the device's system clock for NTP drift. Use commands that display local certificate properties and NTP status. Also confirm basic IP connectivity to vBond with a ping and verify firewall rules that might block control-plane ports. Another common cause is an incorrect System IP or serial number mismatch in vManage; confirm the device registration details match inventory entries. If the certificate has expired or the system clock is wrong, renew the certificate or correct NTP, then attempt re-registration. Always document the exact commands and outputs you used so you can attach them to a support bundle if escalation becomes necessary. Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Device Onboarding
Diagnostic Checklist
  1. Confirm alarm in vManage and note timestamp and device name.
  2. Run show sdwan control connections on the device to verify control status.
  3. Ping vBond from the device to verify basic reachability.
  4. Check NTP synchronization and the certificate status using local properties commands.
  5. Verify System IP and serial number against vManage inventory.
Common Fixes
Correct NTP, reissue or sign certificates, update firewall rules, or fix inventory mismatches.
Example
If show sdwan control local-properties shows an expired certificate and NTP shows drift, set correct NTP, renew the certificate, then reattempt connect.
Pitfall

Skipping inventory checks: a duplicate System IP or wrong serial number in vManage can prevent successful onboarding even if control plane looks healthy.

screens.title: Policy Not Applying or Traffic Not Steering
screens.narratorSegment: When traffic does not follow the intended policy, work methodically. First verify in vManage that the desired policy is activated for the correct site and VPN lists. Activation mistakes are a common cause. Next, on the edge device check the policy as received from vSmart to ensure the device has the expected rules. Use the command that shows policies from vSmart and check for missing or mismatched entries. For control-policy troubleshooting, inspect OMP routes and TLOCs to verify the route attributes—preferences or restrictions may cause different path selection than expected. For data policies like AAR, use application-route statistics on the edge to see which TLOC the application traffic is actually using and whether SLA compliance is being met. Also use the data-policy-filter to confirm traffic is matching your rules. Remember: a policy not activated or applied to the wrong site is more common than a software bug. Always confirm activation scope and policy targeting first. Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Policy Troubleshooting
Step 1: Activation Check
Confirm the policy is activated in vManage and targeted to the correct site and VPN lists.
Step 2: Device Receipt
Run show sdwan policy from-vsmart to verify the device received the policy.
Step 3: Route Attributes
Check show sdwan omp routes and tlocs to ensure the routes and preferences match policy intent.
Step 4: AAR & App Verification
Use show sdwan app-route statistics to see which TLOC an application uses and whether SLA thresholds are met.
Supporting Commands
  • show sdwan data-policy-filter — confirm traffic match.
  • show sdwan omp routes — confirm control-plane distribution.
Key Takeaway

Incorrect activation or targeting is the most common cause of policies not taking effect. Verify activation scope first before deeper debugging.

screens.title: Poor Application Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Poor application performance can stem from link degradation, incorrect policy, or local congestion. Begin by checking TLOC quality in vManage—latency, jitter, and loss are the metrics that directly affect voice and video. If those metrics look healthy, verify interface utilization and QoS policies on the edge device as congestion may cause packet drops. For AAR-managed applications, use the edge command that reports application-route statistics to see the actual path selections and SLA compliance for that application. If SLA is failing on the chosen path, the application may switch paths; examine route attributes or consider changing thresholds. Also check data-policy filters to confirm traffic classification is correct; misclassification causes the wrong rules to apply. A misconception is to assume the WAN link is always the problem; often the application is misidentified or local queuing is the cause. The practical test is to correlate user reports with timestamps in vManage, then confirm path-specific metrics and per-application stats on the edge device before taking corrective action. Poor Application Performance means correlate user complaints with tloc metrics, app-route statistics, and interface utilization before remediating.. Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › App Performance
Quick Checks
  • Confirm TLOC latency/jitter/loss for the affected path in vManage.
  • Review interface utilization and queue drops on the edge device.
  • Validate AAR configuration and app-route statistics for the app.
Example
Users report voice quality issues. vManage shows jitter spikes on the primary TLOC. App-route stats indicate voice is still using that path and SLA is breached. Mitigate by shifting voice to a better TLOC or adjusting thresholds temporarily while investigating the root cause.
Check Your Understanding

If application-route statistics show expected SLA but users still complain, what other device-level metric should you check? (Hint: interface errors and queue drops.)

screens.title: Software Upgrades and Maintenance
screens.narratorSegment: Software upgrades must be planned and executed with a predictable, phased approach. Start by backing up your vManage configuration and ensuring you have redundant controllers and edge devices available. Upload software images to vManage and stage them; follow Cisco-recommended upgrade paths and sequence controllers first—vManage, then vSmart and vBond—before upgrading edge devices. Use phased activation: test on non-production or limited subsets, monitor for regressions, then expand. Always perform upgrades during maintenance windows and have a rollback image and procedure ready. Collect support bundles before and after upgrades to capture baseline and post-upgrade state. A frequent error is upgrading all devices simultaneously, which risks a fabric-wide outage if something goes wrong. Instead, upgrade incrementally and monitor device and application metrics closely between phases. If you see unexpected alarms, pause and investigate using the troubleshooting steps we've practiced. Document each step and preserve logs to facilitate rapid rollback or vendor escalation. Software Upgrades and Maintenance means back up vmanage, stage images, follow controller-first order, upgrade in phases, and collect support bundles for comparison.. In practical terms, staging, activation order, backups and rollback planning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Software Upgrades
Upgrade Sequence
  1. Backup vManage configuration and collect baseline support bundles.
  2. Upload images to vManage and stage them.
  3. Upgrade controllers in order: vManage → vSmart/vBond → edge devices.
  4. Perform phased activation and monitor closely before proceeding.
Operational Notes
  • Always have a rollback plan and retain the previous images.
  • Do not upgrade all devices at once in production.
  • Collect support bundles pre- and post-upgrade for troubleshooting version-related issues.
Safety Note

Perform upgrades in maintenance windows and ensure redundancy. Backups and rollback procedures protect the fabric from prolonged outages.

screens.title: Support Bundles and When to Escalate
screens.narratorSegment: A support bundle consolidates logs, configurations, and status outputs into a single artifact that accelerates vendor troubleshooting. Use the request support-bundle facility on devices to gather OMP state, interface statistics, logs, and configuration snapshots. Before raising a TAC case, collect the relevant vManage dashboard screenshots, timestamps, event logs, and the support bundle from the affected devices. Include the exact CLI commands you ran and their outputs. This context lets the support engineer reproduce or analyze the issue faster. Know when to escalate: after you have collected local evidence, tried standard remediation steps, and the problem persists or impacts critical services. An important misconception is thinking TAC will run basic checks for you; providing a polished support bundle and timestamped evidence reduces back-and-forth and shortens time to resolution. Finally, keep a record of support-bundle names and storage locations so you can reference them later if similar incidents recur. screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity simulates a vManage alarm for a device showing down. Begin in vManage and identify the WAN Edge list entry and alarm timestamp. Record that time. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how to observe, diagnose, and maintain a Cisco SD-WAN deployment using vManage and device-level tools. We start with the dashboards and reports that give you a live and historical view of device health, TLOC and link quality, and application performance. Then we'll practice common troubleshooting flows: reading alarms, running remote diagnostics from vManage, and using essential CLI show commands on vEdge and cEdge devices. You will also see how to stage software images and perform upgrades safely, and how to collect a support bundle when escalation is required. These operational skills matter because SD-WAN is a dynamic fabric: paths and policies change, certificates and time synchronization affect control-plane trust, and proactive monitoring prevents outages. As an example, you will follow a simulated "device down" scenario where an expired certificate plus NTP drift breaks control connections; learning to trace from the vManage alarm to CLI checks shortens mean time to repair. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the right dashboard or CLI command for the problem, perform safe upgrades, and collect diagnostic artifacts for deeper analysis. Remember: good monitoring replaces guesswork with data.

These objectives map directly to practical operations you will perform on Cisco SD-WAN. First, you will learn to use vManage dashboards and reports to observe fabric health, identify overloaded links, and collect historical trends for capacity planning. As a concrete example, you will run a report to show application usage over a week and identify bandwidth hogs. Second, you will identify the key metrics that signal problems: C P U and memory on devices, TLOC latency/jitter/packet loss, and SLA compliance for applications. Third, you will use the suite of troubleshooting tools in vManage—event logs, alarms, real-time monitoring, and remote diagnostics—and know when to escalate to CLI checks on an edge device. Finally, you will perform software staging and upgrades from vManage and collect support bundles for TAC. Each objective pairs a command or UI area with a real operational scenario so you build competence, not just familiarity. As you progress, verify milestone checks documented under "VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE" to confirm you can reproduce the steps independently.

This second objectives slide emphasizes scenario-driven application. You will practice diagnosing a device that fails to join the fabric, verifying policy application when traffic is not steering correctly, and tracing performance degradations for a specific application. Each exercise links a vManage area or CLI command to the observable symptom: for example, use vManage event logs and the WAN Edge list to find a device alarm, then use the device command that checks control connections to confirm whether certificates or NTP are the culprit. You will also validate AAR behavior by using the edge device's application-route statistics to confirm which path an application uses and whether SLA classes are met. Finally, you'll rehearse safe upgrade steps: upload image, stage to a subset of devices, monitor, and roll forward or back depending on results. These skills ensure when something goes wrong you can reduce risk, document findings, and escalate with the right evidence.

vManage dashboards are your single pane of glass into the SD-WAN fabric. A dashboard groups widgets that surface device health, control-plane connectivity, TLOC and WAN link statistics, application SLA compliance, and alarms. Think of dashboards as both a daily operations cockpit and an incident triage map: they help you spot failing devices, saturated interfaces, and applications missing their SLAs. For example, when you see a spike in jitter on a TLOC color used for voice, that single widget points you to the affected sites and the time window for deeper investigation. Dashboards are customizable. You will build or adjust them to surface the metrics you care about, such as C P U thresholds or particular application classes. A common misconception is that dashboards alone resolve incidents; they do not. Dashboards show where to look, not how to fix it. Use dashboards first to narrow scope, then gather logs and run real-time diagnostics. In practice, pair a dashboard alarm with a time-correlated support bundle or CLI output before making configuration changes. How might you tune a dashboard to reduce false positives while still catching real degradation?

Knowing which metrics to monitor lets you separate noise from signal. At the device level focus on C P U and memory utilization and interface status: sustained high C P U often precedes control-plane problems, and interface errors point to physical or routing issues. For link quality monitor TLOC metrics—latency, jitter, and packet loss—for each TLOC color because AAR uses these values to make path choices. Application performance requires SLA compliance metrics and application-route statistics so you can verify whether an application meets its latency and loss targets. A useful monitoring process is to set thresholds and watch both instantaneous values and trends: a single spike may be transient, while a gradual increase in packet loss signals a degrading link. A common misconception is that high utilization always means failure. Instead, correlate utilization with errors and SLA breaches before reconfiguring. For example, 80 percent interface utilization with low packet loss may be acceptable, but 20 percent packet loss at the same time is not. Regularly export reports for trend analysis and capacity planning. Key Metrics to Monitor means use cpu/memory, interface errors, tloc latency/jitter/loss, and sla compliance as core indicators; always correlate metrics before action.. In practical terms, device health, link quality, and application performance indicators. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

vManage centralizes several troubleshooting capabilities that speed triage. Event logs and alarms aggregate significant occurrences across controllers and edge devices: filter them by severity, device, or time to find root events like certificate failures or control connection losses. Real-time monitoring exposes live graphs of interface utilization, C P U/memory, and TLOC metrics; this helps distinguish transient spikes from sustained problems. A powerful time-saver is remote diagnostics from vManage: you can trigger a ping, traceroute, or even a packet capture on an edge device without SSHing into it. That reduces context switching and preserves a documented trail. However, not all fixes are possible from vManage. In complex cases you must SSH to the edge CLI for commands that show OMP routes, TLOCs, and app-route statistics. A common misconception is thinking remote diagnostics replace CLI checks; instead they complement them. Use vManage to gather evidence quickly, then move to device CLI when you need detailed show output or interactive troubleshooting. Which types of incidents would you always start with vManage tools? vManage Troubleshooting Tools means use logs and remote diagnostics for fast evidence collection, then escalate to cli when deeper data or interactive commands are needed.. In practical terms, event logs, alarms, real-time graphs, and remote diagnostics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The edge device CLI provides definitive state for control, routing, and application metrics. First, use the command that checks control connections to confirm whether the device has active DTLS or TLS sessions to vSmart and vBond; this reveals whether the control plane is up. A helpful mental model is to treat vManage as your 'evidence collector' and CLI as your 'repair console.' A device failing to join the fabric is a frequent operational incident. Start by confirming the vManage WAN Edge list or alarm shows the device as down. Next, run the control connections check on the device to see whether DTLS/TLS sessions to vSmart and vBond are up. If the show output indicates "certificate invalid" or similar, verify the certificate status and the device's system clock for NTP drift. Use commands that display local certificate properties and NTP status. Also confirm basic IP connectivity to vBond with a ping and verify firewall rules that might block control-plane ports. Another common cause is an incorrect System IP or serial number mismatch in vManage; confirm the device registration details match inventory entries. If the certificate has expired or the system clock is wrong, renew the certificate or correct NTP, then attempt re-registration. Poor application performance can stem from link degradation, incorrect policy, or local congestion. Begin by checking TLOC quality in vManage—latency, jitter, and loss are the metrics that directly affect voice and video. If those metrics look healthy, verify interface utilization and QoS policies on the edge device as congestion may cause packet drops. For AAR-managed applications, use the edge command that reports application-route statistics to see the actual path selections and SLA compliance for that application. If SLA is failing on the chosen path, the application may switch paths; examine route attributes or consider changing thresholds. Also check data-policy filters to confirm traffic classification is correct; misclassification causes the wrong rules to apply. Software upgrades must be planned and executed with a predictable, phased approach. Start by backing up your vManage configuration and ensuring you have redundant controllers and edge devices available. Upload software images to vManage and stage them; follow Cisco-recommended upgrade paths and sequence controllers first—vManage, then vSmart and vBond—before upgrading edge devices. Use phased activation: test on non-production or limited subsets, monitor for regressions, then expand. Always perform upgrades during maintenance windows and have a rollback image and procedure ready. Collect support bundles before and after upgrades to capture baseline and post-upgrade state. A frequent error is upgrading all devices simultaneously, which risks a fabric-wide outage if something goes wrong. Instead, upgrade incrementally and monitor device and application metrics closely between phases. If you see unexpected alarms, pause and investigate using the troubleshooting steps we've practiced.
